newsitem.title: USA: Tax cuts remain a hurdle in U.S. budget talks.
newsitem.headline: Tax cuts remain a hurdle in U.S. budget talks.

text.p: Talk of movement toward a tax cut compromise surfaced Thursday, but Republicans and Democrats will have to stretch far more to overcome this hurdle in budget negotiations.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott acknowledged that the nearly $200 billion in tax cuts over five years initially sought by Senate Republicans was unlikely to pan out.

In a step toward Democrats, Lott said Republicans "could live with" a five-year tax cut of $140 billion. "They (Democrats) are still wanting less than we can agree to," the Mississippi Republican said.

President Clinton in his budget proposed gross tax cuts of $98 billion over five years, and Senate Democrat Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota has drawn the line at $100 billion, saying he would oppose larger cuts in federal revenues.
The figures mentioned did not take into account any offsetting tax increases. Budget negotiations between the White House and congressional Republicans have yet to explore the tax cut issue in depth.

House Republicans have not publicly put out a tax cut target. The chairman of the House tax-writing committee, Rep. Bill Archer of Texas, has said he wanted to be given an aggregate figure so that his House Ways and Means Committee could work to "fill in the blanks" with specific proposals.
"I don't think there's any magic to any specific number," Archer said earlier this week.
On the other side of the Capitol, the chief of the Senate tax-writing panel said he was sticking to his guns of wanting a net tax cut of $140 billion.
"I feel very strongly we need a net tax cut in the area of $140 billion," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said.

Roth has put forward a plan that would cut taxes a total of $178 billion over five years, offset by $35 billion in tax increases -- $30 billion from the airline ticket tax and $5 billion of the revenue raisers proposed by Clinton.
Clinton has proposed a total of $76 billion in offsets to his tax cut for a net tax reduction of $22 billion.
Archer, a key player in tax policy because all tax legislation must originate in his committee, has said, "I do not believe we can raise revenues in excess of $5 billion over five years."
Democrats say Republicans want higher tax cuts to benefit the wealthy at the expense of cutting spending on social programs for the elderly and poor.
Republicans have indicated a willingness to negotiate on some specific tax issues, with a broad-based capital gains tax cut their priority and a tax credit for higher education Clinton's priority.
Republicans have also staked out a position on wanting to eliminate the estate tax. Any tax package is expected to include a child credit, which both Republicans and Democrats appear to support.
